newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end up, except for gold.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end up, except for gold.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended higher Tuesday, except for gold which slipped on news the German government compromised with the Bundesbank on its plan to revalue the bank's gold reserves to help Germany meet European Monetary Union (EMU) criteria.

"The revaluation plan had originally been seen as slightly positive because it made actual gold sales less likely, so news of a deferral of the plan had the opposite effect," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.

"But the Germans have always said they are not planning to actually sell gold anyway, and the dispute has illustrated how difficult it would be for a major European country to actually sell down its gold reserves significantly, which is bullish for gold longer term," he said.
COMEX August gold ended down $0.80 at $345.70 an ounce after trading from $347.10 to $345.00. Estimated volume was only 16,000 lots.
Spot gold ended quoted at $343.00/50 against the London afternoon fix of $343.55 and Monday's New York finish of $343.30/70.
Meanwhile, COMEX July silver ended up 3.0 cents at $4.728 an ounce, after seeing a $4.690-4.745 range.

In news Tuesday, Germany said it would defer until 1998 its controversial plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves, but German Finance Minister Waigel said Germany would qualify for EMU using spending cuts and privatization revenues.
Analysts said the Bundesbank had clearly won the showdown with Bonn, and this augured well for the strength of the euro, if it is introduced in 1999.
Earlier in 1991 the Bundesbank lost the battle over terms for monetary unification of East and West Germany, forcing the resignation of then Bundesbank president Karl Otto Pohl.
The German government this year faces a budget deficit of about 19 billion marks ($11 billion) in 1997, or about 3.3 percent of GDP.
To meet EMU criteria, EU-country fiscal deficits must be reduced to 3.0 percent of GDP and debt cut to 60 pct of GDP.

Waigel planned to use a revaluation of Bundesbank gold to to raise an accounting profit of about 10 billion marks, or about 0.3 percent of GDP, to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio, thus reducing interest costs and the budget deficit.
Bundesbank gold reserves total about 95 million ounces, valued in the books at 144 marks per ounce, against a market value of about 600 marks an ounce.

Marking the reserves to market would have produced a revaluation gain of about 40 billion marks ($24 billion), of which about 20 billion marks would be transferred over two years, by way of a Bundesbank special dividend, to the government's Inherited Debt Redemption Fund to reduce debt.

The Bundesbank was not opposed in principle to revaluing its gold reserves as Germany, Sweden and Luxembourg are the only remaining countries in Europe with reserves in the books at well-below-market rates.

But the central argued against the plan because of the implications for money supply growth, and because of the threat to confidence in the new euro currency resulting from indulging in dubious accounting practices. Germany had earlier insisted on strict compliance with the Maastricht Treaty criteria by other countries.
Under accounting rules issued by the EU Statistical Office, one-off asset sales or realised capital gains may be used to reduce a debt-to-GDP ratio, but are not admissible to reduce a budget deficit.
However, the Brussels' statisticians have not yet ruled on unrealized capital gains or revaluations and the central banks of France and Italy have indulged in revaluations earlier.
Meanwhile, in platinum group metals (PGM) Tuesday, renewed tightness in the physical market and some pressure on deliveries of the NYMEX June palladium contract saw PGM futures end higher.

NYMEX June palladium ended up $13.85 an ounce at $181.65, while the now-active September contract gained $5.35 to $169.65. NYMEX June palladium's first notice day was Monday and the contract expires on June 25.
NYMEX July platinum ended up $3.00 at $401.70 an ounce.

In the physical market, one month palladium lending rates soared to around 75 percent, from around 30 percent Monday, and short term platinum lending rates jumped to around 40 percent from 25 percent Monday.
Russian exports of PGMs have been suspended since last December, forcing a drawdown of world inventories.
But about 15 Japanese trade houses are now in talks with Russian officials over a resumption of exports.

Russia is the world's largest supplier of palladium, but the U.S. has now surpassed Japan as the leading consumer, according to a report last month by refiners Johnson Matthey. ((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641))
